title: Jamia Promises Union Polls After 20 Years and Revokes Suspensions; Students Reject Offer
excerpt: Jamia's October 26 order ties elections to approval of the union constitution with no deadline, revokes suspensions and promises a security inquiry — students call it ambiguous and vow to continue protesting.
body:
• Jamia Millia Islamia's October 26 order promises students' union elections 15 days after approval of the union constitution — the first polls since the union was dissolved in 2006 — and revokes protest-related suspensions and show-cause notices.
  • Protesting students have rejected the order as ambiguous, saying it gives no deadline for approving the constitution and therefore no real election date, and objecting to a public apology condition recorded in the order.
  • The order also promises a committee to inquire into security staff conduct during the agitation, but does not address the demand for the Proctor's resignation.
  • Classes remain online after the university's October 24 move, so Jamia students should watch for a written election timeline rather than treating the October 26 order as a settled return to normal.

Jamia Millia Islamia has promised to hold students' union elections and revoke protest-related suspensions, but protesting students rejected the offer on Monday, October 26, calling it ambiguous and vowing to continue their agitation. The order is the newest development in a protest that prompted the university on October 24 to move all classes online — a step The Videshi covered at the time — and it still leaves the central dispute unresolved.

What the Administration Offered

In an order dated October 26, the university said, according to ANI reporting carried by Devdiscourse: "The Jamia Millia Islamia Students' Union Election will be held after 15 days from the date of approval of the constitution of the students' union of Jamia Millia Islamia." The students' union was dissolved in 2006, so the promise would restore elected student representation after about 20 years.

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2114617914129355224

The order also revoked suspension orders and show-cause notices issued to students during the protest and said a committee would be constituted to inquire into the actions of security staff during the agitation. Registrar Prof. Md Mahtab Alam Rizvi arrived on campus at about 4:30 a.m. on Monday to meet protesting students, shared the order and urged them to call off the agitation, saying their demands had been met. The administration directed that the protest be called off immediately on issue of the order.

The order further recorded that protesting students had agreed to issue a public apology through a press conference for "defamatory statements/actions/posts" against the administration and to take such posts down from social media with immediate effect.

Why Students Rejected It

Students said the order provides no definite timeline for approving the constitution, and therefore no definite election date. The Jammu and Kashmir Students' Association said, in a statement reported by ANI: "The notice failed to provide a clear and unambiguous announcement regarding the restoration of the students' union, leaving several key concerns unaddressed." Students also pointed out that the order does not address their demand for the resignation of the Proctor.

The apology condition drew a direct rejection from hunger strikers. Careers360 reported Ebin Basil, a student on hunger strike, saying in a video shared by Millat Times English that students faced pressure to sign, and asking why they should apologise.

"Why should we apologise? We are not criminals. We haven't committed any crime."

— Ebin Basil, hunger-striking student, quoted by Millat Times English via Careers360

Basil said the students had protested peacefully, that their demands remained unmet and that the protest would continue. Careers360 also reported that students, including hunger strikers Ebin Basil and Rehan Khan, continued to oppose the conditions and argued that an election date should be announced.

Background: Two Weeks of Protest, Classes Online

The agitation has run for nearly two weeks, including a hunger strike demanding restoration of the elected students' body, withdrawal of disciplinary action and accountability for security staff conduct. On October 24, the university shifted all classes online until further notice, citing student safety and continuity of academic activities, and ordered closure of the Dr Zakir Husain Library and the Old Library. Those operational steps remain the backdrop to Monday's order; the reports do not announce a return to in-person classes.

What Happens Next

The dispute now turns on a single missing piece: a deadline for approving the union constitution. Without it, the 15-day election clock in the October 26 order never starts. Students say they will continue until demands are addressed through clear, written commitments, including a concrete roadmap for elections. ANI reported it sought comment from the university's press department and had received no response at the time of filing. Until the administration supplies the approval timeline — or students accept the order as written — Jamia's classes, library access and campus protest remain in the same unsettled state that prompted the online move on October 24.
